summary:
Ryan Dahl opens by describing Deno Deploy, an incidents-and-pager service where OpenClaw and other agents now resolve many incidents that previously paged a human. To make this effective, Deno grants these agents broad read/write access to Postgres, Kubernetes, ClickHouse, AWS, GitHub, and Slack. Dahl acknowledges the danger of destructive actions like a psql-driven DROP TABLE or a Kubernetes namespace deletion. While Opus is well aligned and refuses such orders, Dahl argues that relying on model obedience is wishful thinking because agents are reachable through the support system and can be prompt-injected. Deno's stance is that the agent is untrusted software, including its own security plugins or modifications, and the guard cannot live inside it.

Agents already run on isolated standalone VMs, so filesystem and syscall concerns are mitigated. The real attack surface is every byte that leaves the agent, often through non-HTTP paths such as psql tunneling through an EKS endpoint into a VPC. Existing controls are insufficient: careful ACLs and readonly credentials are hard to compose across systems, MCP tool permissions break once an agent spawns a subprocess, LLM gateways only see provider traffic, HTTP-layer proxies like HTTP Jail and Crabtrap miss non-HTTP protocols, agent-vault-style credential injection is necessary but incomplete, and process sandboxes like Nvidia OpenShell address a layer Deno does not need.

Claw Patrol is Deno's MIT-licensed answer: a byte-level egress proxy that parses protocols like Postgres, holds and injects credentials (cookies, OAuth, AWS SigV4), and enforces rules written in HCL, the Terraform configuration language, stored in git and unit tested against fixture requests. Deno's own rule file is roughly a thousand lines, and Claw Patrol has its own large test suite. The proxy can reject, route to an LLM judge, or request human approval in Slack, or chain both. A recorded demo shows Codex in yolo mode obeying an order to delete the users table, with Claw Patrol killing the action at the Postgres wire protocol. Claw Patrol runs over Tailscale (used as an exit node and dashboard auth) or WireGuard. Dahl closes by predicting the problem shrinks as models get smarter and gain better context, but that backstop security mechanisms will always be required because AI can never be fully trusted.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Deno Deploy incidents
sections.summary: Ryan Dahl introduces himself, describes Deno Deploy and its pager, and explains that agents like OpenClaw are now used to automatically service incidents, with read/write access to Postgres, Kubernetes, ClickHouse, AWS, GitHub, and Slack.

sections.title: Why model obedience is not enough
sections.summary: Dahl notes Opus is well aligned and refuses to drop the users table, but argues this is insufficient because the agent is connected to the support system and can be prompt-injected. The agent must be treated as untrusted software and the guard cannot live inside it.

sections.title: Every action is bytes on the wire
sections.summary: Agents run on standalone VMs so filesystem concerns are limited; the real surface is every byte leaving the agent, including non-HTTP protocols like Postgres reached via psql subprocess. The hard case is tunneling through an EKS endpoint into a VPC.

sections.title: Why existing controls fall short
sections.summary: ACLs and readonly credentials are hard to compose across systems. MCP tool permissions break once an agent spawns a subprocess. LLM gateways, HTTP-layer proxies (HTTP Jail, Crabtrap), credential injectors (Agent Vault), and process sandboxes (Nvidia OpenShell) each cover only part of the problem.

sections.title: Introducing Claw Patrol and HCL rules
sections.summary: Claw Patrol is an MIT-licensed byte-level egress proxy that parses protocols, holds and injects credentials, and applies HCL rules checked into git. Deno's production rule file is about a thousand lines, with example rules blocking certain Postgres functions and a plug-in system for new protocols.

sections.title: Demo: blocking a users-table drop
sections.summary: A recorded demo runs Codex in yolo mode, tells it to delete the users table, and shows Claw Patrol parsing the Postgres wire bytes and rejecting the destructive action. A dashboard shows per-agent traffic, denied requests, and pending approvals.

sections.title: Approvals, credentials, and Tailscale deployment
sections.summary: Rules can route actions to an LLM judge, a human in Slack, or both, treating the agent as a black box. Claw Patrol injects credentials for cookies, OAuth, Postgres, ClickHouse, and AWS SigV4 so the agent never sees secrets. It runs over Tailscale (exit node plus dashboard auth) or WireGuard.

sections.title: Closing thesis: agents cannot police themselves
sections.summary: Dahl reiterates that because Claw Patrol itself holds production credentials it must be carefully secured, and the core thesis is that agents cannot be trusted to police their own behavior.

sections.title: Q&A: testing the rule file and whether the problem shrinks
sections.summary: Dahl answers two audience questions. First, testing is done via a unit-test system built into the HCL rule file that runs fixture requests against the rules, alongside a large Claw Patrol test suite. Second, smarter models with better context and stronger alignment (such as Opus) reduce but never eliminate the problem; backstop security mechanisms will always be needed because AI cannot be fully trusted.

demonstrations: Codex run in yolo mode is told to delete the users table from Postgres, spawns psql, and is blocked by Claw Patrol at the Postgres wire protocol after the proxy parses and applies its rules.
Claw Patrol dashboard view shows agents, the requests flowing through, denied actions, and actions pending approval, with click-through detail per action.
limitations: Opus model alignment alone is insufficient because agents can be prompt-injected through connected systems like support.
ACLs, readonly credentials, and careful provisioning are hard to compose across many systems and leave holes.
MCP tool permissions cannot stop an agent that spawns psql or another subprocess, breaking the security boundary.
LLM gateways only inspect traffic to LLM providers and miss database and other non-LLM protocols.
HTTP-layer proxies like HTTP Jail and Crabtrap operate above the non-HTTP protocols agents commonly use.
Process sandboxes such as Nvidia OpenShell guard filesystem and syscalls but are unnecessary when agents already run on isolated VMs.
Security plugins or modifications inside the agent itself cannot be trusted; the security boundary must live elsewhere.
Claw Patrol itself holds production credentials and must be tightly secured.
Even with smarter models, AI can never be fully trusted, so backstop security mechanisms will always be needed.
